questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 4 · Firm and firm name
questions.stem: Under the Indian Partnership Act 1932, which statement about a 'firm' is correct?

readLink.label: Read: What a partnership is, s. 4 →

options.text: A firm is a legal person distinct from its partners from the moment the partnership agreement is signed
options.explanation: This borrows the rule for companies. Separate legal personality follows incorporation under the Companies Act 2013; no such personality is conferred by the Partnership Act.

options.text: A firm becomes a legal person only when it is registered under section 59
options.explanation: Registration under s. 59 records the firm in the Register of Firms; it does not create a legal person, and s. 69 is the only real consequence of failing to register.

options.text: A firm is a legal person for the purposes of contract but not for the purposes of taxation
options.explanation: This inverts the true position: the firm is treated as a separate entity for accounting and tax computation, but it remains no legal person in contract.

options.text: A firm is only the collective name for the persons who have entered into partnership; it has no legal personality separate from the partners
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 defines partners collectively as 'a firm'; the firm is a compendious name, not a legal person, so its debts are the partners' debts.

questions.stem: Three brothers carry on the ancestral cloth business of their Hindu undivided family. Are they partners in that business?

readLink.label: Read: The five essentials and mutual agency, s. 4 →

options.text: Yes, because they share the profits of a business carried on by all of them
options.explanation: This applies s. 4 without reading s. 5. Profit-sharing within a family business springs from status by birth, not from any agreement.

options.text: No, because the relation of partnership arises from contract and not from status
options.explanation: Correct. Section 5 says so in terms, and expressly names members of an HUF carrying on a family business as not being partners in that business.

options.text: Yes, but only if the karta consents in writing to their being treated as partners
options.explanation: No consent of the karta converts coparcenary into partnership; only a fresh contract between them could, and then it would be a new firm.

options.text: No, because a Hindu undivided family business is not a 'business' within section 2(b)
options.explanation: The reason given is wrong. An HUF business is plainly a business; what is missing is the agreement required by s. 5.

questions.stem: The 'true test' of partnership, applied by courts where the facts are disputed, is:

readLink.label: Read: The five essentials and mutual agency, s. 4 →

options.text: Mutual agency — that the business is carried on by all or any of them acting for all
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 requires the business to be carried on 'by all or any of them acting for all', and s. 18 makes each partner an agent of the firm.

options.text: The sharing of profits in an agreed ratio
options.explanation: Profit-sharing is an essential, but the Explanation to s. 6 says its receipt is not of itself conclusive that the receiver is a partner.

options.text: The existence of a registered partnership deed
options.explanation: A deed is evidence and registration is optional; neither is a test of the relation, which may be inferred from conduct alone.

options.text: The contribution of capital by every person alleged to be a partner
options.explanation: Capital is not an essential at all. A partner may contribute skill or labour only and still be a partner.

questions.stem: Hemant lends ₹10,00,000 to a firm and, instead of fixed interest, is paid 20% of its annual profits until repayment. He takes no part in the business. Hemant is:

readLink.label: Read: Deciding whether a partnership exists, s. 6 →

options.text: A partner, because he shares in the profits of a business carried on by the firm
options.explanation: This treats profit-sharing as conclusive. Section 6 requires the real relation to be judged on all the facts, and the missing element is mutual agency.

options.text: A partner in profits only, liable to third parties but not for losses
options.explanation: A partner in profits only is a real partner whose profit share is an entitlement as a member of the firm; Hemant's share is the return on a loan.

options.text: Not a partner, because the receipt of a share of profits by a lender does not of itself make him a partner
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 6 expressly covers a lender who receives a share of profits, and Hemant has no power to bind the firm.

options.text: Not a partner, because he does not share the losses of the firm
options.explanation: The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong: sharing losses is not an essential of partnership, and a partner may be indemnified against losses.

questions.stem: Two sisters inherit a warehouse and let it out, dividing the rent equally. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Partnership distinguished from look-alikes →

options.text: They are co-owners, not partners, because there is no business carried on and neither can bind the other
options.explanation: Correct. Co-ownership may arise by inheritance without any agreement, needs no business, and carries no mutual agency.

options.text: They are partners, because they share the income of jointly held property
options.explanation: Sharing the income of jointly held property is sharing gross returns, and there is no business being carried on as required by s. 4.

options.text: They are partners at will, since no term has been fixed for their arrangement
options.explanation: Section 7 can only classify an existing partnership. It cannot turn co-ownership into one.

options.text: They are co-owners, but each may transfer her share only with the other's consent
options.explanation: The classification is right, the consequence wrong: a co-owner may transfer her share freely, unlike a partner (s. 29).

questions.stem: Which of these is a correct distinction between a partnership firm and a Hindu undivided family business?

readLink.label: Read: Partnership distinguished from look-alikes →

options.text: In an HUF business the coparceners have no liability of any kind for the business debts
options.explanation: Coparceners are liable to the extent of their share in the joint family property; it is only the personal, unlimited liability that is confined to the karta.

options.text: A minor can be a full partner in a firm but cannot be a coparcener until he is 18
options.explanation: This reverses both rules: a minor cannot be a partner (only admitted to benefits under s. 30), while a coparcener acquires his interest by birth.

options.text: In a firm every partner is personally and unlimitedly liable, whereas in an HUF business only the karta is personally liable, the other coparceners being liable to the extent of their share in the family property
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25 imposes joint and several unlimited liability on partners; in an HUF the personal exposure is the karta's.

options.text: Both relations arise from agreement, the only difference being the number of members
options.explanation: Partnership arises from contract; an HUF arises from status. Section 5 makes the distinction expressly.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to a company but NOT to a partnership firm?

readLink.label: Read: Partnership distinguished from look-alikes →

options.text: The ability to carry on a lawful business for profit
options.explanation: Both may carry on a lawful business for profit; this is common ground and not a distinguishing feature.

options.text: Liability of the participants for debts incurred while they were members
options.explanation: Members of a company are liable only to the extent of the unpaid amount on their shares, but some liability exists in both, so this is not the distinguishing feature.

options.text: The requirement that its accounts be kept and its profits shared as agreed
options.explanation: Keeping accounts is common to both, and profit-sharing by agreement is a partnership feature, not a company one.

options.text: Perpetual succession, so that the death or insolvency of a member does not affect the entity's existence
options.explanation: Correct. A firm has no perpetual succession: death or insolvency of a partner affects the firm and may even dissolve it under s. 42.

questions.stem: A partnership is a 'partnership at will' where:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of partnership, ss. 7 and 8 →

options.text: No provision is made for the duration of the partnership, even though the deed fixes how the firm may be ended
options.explanation: A deed that fixes a mode of determination takes the firm out of s. 7, however silent it is about duration.

options.text: No provision is made by contract between the partners for the duration of their partnership and no provision is made for its determination
options.explanation: Correct. Section 7 requires BOTH the absence of a fixed duration and the absence of any agreed mode of determination.

options.text: The partners have expressly agreed that any of them may retire at any time
options.explanation: An express clause about retirement is a provision for determination, which is the very thing that prevents s. 7 applying.

options.text: The firm is unregistered, since registration alone fixes the duration of a firm
options.explanation: Registration has nothing to do with duration; the s. 58 statement records the duration, it does not create it.

questions.stem: Four persons form a firm solely to construct one bridge under a single contract with the State. Which is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of partnership, ss. 7 and 8 →

options.text: It is a particular partnership under section 8, and subject to contract it is dissolved on the completion of the undertaking
options.explanation: Correct. Section 8 recognises a partnership for a particular adventure or undertaking, and s. 42(b) dissolves it on completion.

options.text: It is a partnership at will, because no period of years has been fixed
options.explanation: The venture itself fixes the duration, so there is a provision for duration and s. 7 does not apply.

options.text: It is not a partnership at all, because a single venture is not a 'business'
options.explanation: A single venture is enough; s. 8 assumes it and 'business' in s. 2(b) includes every trade or occupation.

options.text: It is a partnership that can be dissolved only by an order of the court under section 44
options.explanation: Section 44 lists grounds on which a court may dissolve any firm; it is not the only route out of a particular partnership.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Kinds of partners · Sleeping partner
questions.stem: A dormant (sleeping) partner retires from a firm without any public notice being given. As regards acts of the firm done after his retirement, he is:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of partners →

options.text: Liable, because section 32(3) makes every retiring partner liable until public notice is given
options.explanation: The general rule is stated correctly but the proviso is missed: it exempts a partner who was unknown to the person dealing with the firm.

options.text: Not liable, because a retiring partner who was not known to the person dealing with the firm to be a partner is outside the rule that liability continues until public notice
options.explanation: Correct. The outsider never gave credit on the faith of his membership, so the proviso protects him.

options.text: Liable, unless he also gives individual written notice to every existing creditor
options.explanation: No individual notice is required of a dormant partner at all; the exemption applies without any notice.

options.text: Not liable, because a dormant partner is never liable for the debts of the firm
options.explanation: The conclusion happens to be right but the reason is badly wrong: a dormant partner is fully liable for debts incurred while he was a partner.

questions.stem: Partner Lalit agrees to give his friend Mohit one-half of Lalit's own share of the firm's profits. Mohit's position is that he:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of partners →

options.text: Becomes a partner in the firm to the extent of the share transferred to him
options.explanation: A person becomes a partner only with the consent of all the partners (s. 31); one partner cannot admit another by private arrangement.

options.text: May inspect the books of the firm and require accounts, though he cannot take part in management
options.explanation: Even a transferee under s. 29 cannot require accounts or inspect books while the firm continues, and a sub-partner has less than that.

options.text: Is liable to the firm's creditors to the extent of the profits he receives
options.explanation: He has no privity with the firm's creditors; the liability for firm debts stays with the partners under s. 25.

options.text: Has no rights against the firm at all and cannot demand accounts or bind it; his only claim is against Lalit
options.explanation: Correct. A sub-partner is a stranger to the firm: no agency, no liability for its debts, no right to its books.

questions.stem: Nikhil is admitted as a partner on 1 July 2026 with the consent of all the existing partners. A supplier sues in August 2026 for goods delivered to the firm in March 2026. Nikhil is:

readLink.label: Read: Changes in the constitution, ss. 31 to 38 →

options.text: Liable, because section 25 makes every partner jointly and severally liable for all the debts of the firm
options.explanation: Section 25 is limited to acts of the firm done 'while he is a partner'. March 2026 was before Nikhil joined.

options.text: Liable to the extent of the capital he has brought in, but not personally
options.explanation: There is no such halfway rule for past debts. He is either liable in full, if he assumed the debt, or not at all.

options.text: Not liable, because a person introduced as a partner does not thereby become liable for any act of the firm done before he became a partner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 31(2) says exactly this; only a fresh agreement with the creditor (novation) could make him liable for the past.

options.text: Not liable, provided he gives public notice of his admission within a reasonable time
options.explanation: No public notice is required on admission, and his freedom from past debts does not depend on giving one.

questions.stem: Which of the following must a creditor prove to fix a non-partner with liability under section 28?

readLink.label: Read: Partner by holding out, s. 28 →

options.text: That the defendant represented himself, or knowingly permitted himself to be represented, as a partner, and that the creditor gave credit to the firm on the faith of that representation
options.explanation: Correct. Representation plus knowing permission plus credit given on the faith of it are the elements of holding out.

options.text: That the defendant actually shared in the profits of the firm during the period of credit
options.explanation: A holding-out partner takes no profits at all; that is precisely why he gets no rights against the firm in return.

options.text: That the defendant knew his name had reached the particular creditor before credit was given
options.explanation: Section 28(1) says the opposite in terms: it is immaterial whether he knew the representation had reached the person giving credit.

options.text: That the firm was registered and the defendant's name appeared in the Register of Firms
options.explanation: Registration is irrelevant to s. 28, which works by estoppel and applies to registered and unregistered firms alike.

questions.stem: After the death of partner Suresh, the firm continues under the old name 'Suresh & Co'. A creditor who supplies goods to the firm in 2026 sues Suresh's estate. The estate is:

readLink.label: Read: Partner by holding out, s. 28 →

options.text: Liable, because the firm name amounts to a continuing representation that Suresh is a partner
options.explanation: This is the very argument s. 28(2) rules out; a dead man's name in the style of the firm is not a representation binding his estate.

options.text: Liable, unless the legal representative published a public notice of the death
options.explanation: No public notice is required on death, and s. 35 already frees the estate from acts done after death.

options.text: Not liable, because the continued use of the deceased partner's name as part of the firm name does not of itself make his legal representative liable for acts of the firm done after his death
options.explanation: Correct. Section 28(2) protects the estate expressly, even though the name stays on the board.

options.text: Not liable, provided the estate has already been fully distributed among the heirs
options.explanation: The conclusion is right for the wrong reason: distribution of the estate is irrelevant, since no liability attaches in the first place.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30(1) · Admission of a minor
questions.stem: Which statement about a minor and a partnership firm is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Minor admitted to the benefits, s. 30 →

options.text: A minor may become a full partner if his guardian signs the deed on his behalf
options.explanation: A guardian cannot make a minor a partner, because the minor's own agreement would be void under s. 11 of the Contract Act.

options.text: A minor may, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, be admitted to the benefits of partnership in an existing firm
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(1) requires an existing firm and the consent of every partner; the minor is never made a partner.

options.text: A firm may be constituted between one major and one minor, the minor taking the benefits only
options.explanation: There must be an existing firm of at least two competent persons before a minor can be admitted to its benefits.

options.text: A minor may be admitted to the benefits with the consent of a majority of the partners
options.explanation: Section 30(1) requires the consent of all the partners for the time being, not a majority.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30(2) · Minor's right of inspection
questions.stem: A minor admitted to the benefits of a firm demands to see its records. He is entitled to inspect and copy:

readLink.label: Read: Minor admitted to the benefits, s. 30 →

options.text: Any of the books of the firm, on the same footing as a partner
options.explanation: That is the partner's right under s. 12(d). The minor's right is deliberately narrower.

options.text: Nothing at all, since he has no right of management
options.explanation: He has no management rights, but s. 30(2) does give him access to the accounts.

options.text: Only the account recording his own share of profits
options.explanation: The section is not limited to his own account; it extends to any of the accounts of the firm.

options.text: Any of the accounts of the firm, but not its other books
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(2) confines the minor to the accounts, whereas s. 12(d) gives a partner access to any of the books of the firm.

questions.stem: The six-month period within which a former minor may elect to become, or not to become, a partner runs from:

readLink.label: Read: The six-month election, s. 30(5) →

options.text: The date he attains majority, in every case
options.explanation: This drops the second limb of s. 30(5), which exists because a minor is often admitted without knowing of it.

options.text: The later of the date he attains majority and the date he obtains knowledge that he had been admitted to the benefits of partnership
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(5) fixes the trigger as whichever of the two dates is later.

options.text: The date the other partners call upon him in writing to make his election
options.explanation: No such call is required or recognised; the clock runs from majority or knowledge, whichever is later.

options.text: The earlier of the date he attains majority and the date he learns of his admission
options.explanation: The section says the later of the two dates, not the earlier; taking the earlier date shortens his window wrongly.

questions.stem: A former minor becomes a partner on the expiry of the six-month period. His personal liability to third parties extends to acts of the firm done:

readLink.label: Read: The six-month election, s. 30(5) →

options.text: Since the date he attained majority
options.explanation: This is the commonest error. Majority starts the election clock; it does not fix the start of his liability.

options.text: Since the date the six-month period expired
options.explanation: That is when he becomes a partner, but the section deliberately reaches back to the date of admission to the benefits.

options.text: Since the date he was admitted to the benefits of partnership
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(7)(b) is retrospective to the date of admission to the benefits, not to majority or to the date of election.

options.text: Only from the date on which a public notice of his election is published
options.explanation: He gave no public notice at all in this case, and even where notice is given the liability under s. 30(7)(b) reaches back.

questions.stem: Ishan was admitted to the benefits of a firm on 10 June 2022. He attained majority on 12 March 2026 but came to know of his admission only on 20 July 2026. The last date on which he may give public notice of his election is:

readLink.label: Read: The six-month election, s. 30(5) →

options.text: 20 January 2027
options.explanation: Correct. The clock runs from the later of majority (12 March 2026) and knowledge (20 July 2026), so six months from 20 July 2026 ends on 20 January 2027.

options.text: 12 September 2026
options.explanation: This runs the six months from the date of majority, ignoring the second limb of s. 30(5) which takes the later of the two dates.

options.text: 10 December 2022
options.explanation: This runs the period from the date of admission to the benefits, which is not a trigger under s. 30(5) at all.

options.text: 20 July 2027
options.explanation: This allows twelve months instead of six; the period in s. 30(5) is six months.

questions.stem: Two partners have no written deed. One works in the business full time; the other does nothing but has contributed the capital. In the absence of any agreement:

readLink.label: Read: Rights, duties and defaults, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.text: The working partner is entitled to reasonable remuneration before profits are divided
options.explanation: The Act gives no default salary; remuneration must be agreed, and the deed here is silent.

options.text: Profits are shared in the ratio of capital contributed, since only one partner brought capital
options.explanation: Capital ratio is not the default. Section 13(b) makes the sharing equal regardless of unequal capitals.

options.text: The working partner is entitled to remuneration, and the other to interest on capital at 6% per annum
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: no default remuneration, and 6% under s. 13(d) applies to advances beyond capital, not to capital.

options.text: The working partner is entitled to no remuneration, and both share profits equally
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(a) denies remuneration in the absence of agreement and s. 13(b) makes the shares equal.

questions.stem: Kamini agreed to bring ₹5,00,000 as capital and did so. On 1 August 2025 she advanced a further ₹3,00,000 to the firm for its business, and it remained outstanding for 8 months. The deed says nothing about interest, and the firm made a loss for the year. She is entitled to:

readLink.label: Read: Rights, duties and defaults, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.explanation: This applies 6% to the ₹3,00,000 for a full year instead of the eight months for which the advance was outstanding.
This charges 6% on the capital of ₹5,00,000 as well; capital carries interest only if agreed, and then only out of profits (s. 13(c)).

options.text: Nil, because the firm made a loss
options.explanation: This confuses s. 13(d) with s. 13(c). Interest on an advance is a charge against the firm and does not depend on profits.
Correct. Section 13(d) gives 6% p.a. on advances beyond agreed capital, payable whether or not there are profits: ₹3,00,000 × 6% × 8/12 = ₹12,000.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 12(c) · Ordinary matters and change of business
questions.stem: In a firm of five partners dealing in stationery, three partners resolve to switch the firm's business to money-lending. The remaining two object. The resolution is:

readLink.label: Read: Rights, duties and defaults, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.text: Effective, because differences as to any matter connected with the business may be decided by a majority
options.explanation: The majority rule in s. 12(c) is confined to ordinary matters, and the section carves out a change in the nature of the business.

options.text: Effective, provided the two dissenting partners were given a chance to express their opinion
options.explanation: The right to be heard applies to ordinary matters decided by majority; it cannot cure the absence of unanimous consent here.

options.text: Ineffective, because no change may be made in the nature of the business without the consent of all the partners
options.explanation: Correct. Section 12(c) allows a majority to decide ordinary matters only; a change in the nature of the business needs unanimity.

options.text: Ineffective, because a firm can never change the nature of its business once registered
options.explanation: It can, with the consent of all the partners; registration merely requires the change to be notified to the Registrar.

questions.stem: A partner in a firm of pharmaceutical distributors secretly starts, in his own name, a rival pharmaceutical distribution business and earns ₹9,00,000 from it. Subject to contract, the firm may require him to:

readLink.label: Read: Partnership property and personal profits, ss. 14 to 16 →

options.text: Compensate the firm only for the loss it can prove it actually suffered
options.explanation: Section 16(b) is an accounting for profits, not a claim for damages, so no proof of loss is needed.

options.text: Account for and pay to the firm all the profits he made in that business
options.explanation: Correct. Section 16(b) requires the profits of a competing business of the same nature to be handed over, whether or not the firm lost anything.

options.text: Pay over one half of the profits, the other half being his own remuneration for the work
options.explanation: The section makes no allowance for the partner's own effort; all profits of the competing business go to the firm.

options.text: Close the rival business, but keep the profits already earned
options.explanation: An injunction may lie, but s. 16(b) also reaches the profits already made.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 19(2) · Exclusions from implied authority
questions.stem: In the absence of any usage or custom of trade to the contrary, which of these acts is WITHIN a partner's implied authority?

readLink.label: Read: The statutory exclusions, s. 19(2) →

options.text: Engaging a lawyer to defend a suit brought against the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Defending the firm is ordinary business; the s. 19(2) list bars withdrawing a suit, admitting liability and compromising, not defending.

options.text: Submitting a dispute relating to the business of the firm to arbitration
options.explanation: This is the first item in the s. 19(2) list of acts outside implied authority.

options.text: Acquiring immovable property on behalf of the firm
options.explanation: Section 19(2)(f) puts the acquisition of immovable property outside implied authority.

options.text: Opening a banking account on behalf of the firm in the partner's own name
options.explanation: Section 19(2)(b) excludes exactly this, because the firm's money would sit under a personal name.

questions.stem: The deed of a cloth firm bars any partner from placing an order above ₹2,00,000 alone. A partner orders ₹6,50,000 of cloth from a mill that has dealt with the firm for years and knows nothing of the deed. The firm is:

readLink.label: Read: Extending and restricting authority, ss. 20 to 24 →

options.text: Bound, because a restriction on implied authority does not affect a third party who does not know of it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 20 makes an internal restriction ineffective against an outsider unless he knew of it or did not believe the person to be a partner.

options.text: Not bound, because the partner exceeded the authority conferred on him by the deed
options.explanation: The deed governs the partners between themselves; against the mill the act still falls within implied authority.

options.text: Bound only to the extent of ₹2,00,000, the balance being the partner's personal liability
options.explanation: The Act does not split a single contract in this way; the firm is bound for the whole order.

options.text: Not bound, because buying cloth worth more than three times the internal limit cannot be 'in the usual way'
options.explanation: The usual-way test looks at the kind of transaction, not at whether an internal money limit was exceeded.

questions.stem: During a flood a partner hires trucks at three times the normal rate, without the consent required by the deed, to move the firm's stock to safety overnight. Which is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Extending and restricting authority, ss. 20 to 24 →

options.text: The firm is not bound, because the deed required consent and no consent was taken
options.explanation: Section 21 operates in spite of the ordinary limits on authority; that is the whole purpose of an emergency power.

options.text: The firm is bound, but the partner must bear the excess over the normal hire charges himself
options.explanation: The test is what a prudent person would have done in his own case, not the ordinary market rate in calm conditions.

options.text: The firm is bound, because in an emergency a partner may do all acts a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case to protect the firm from loss, and he is indemnified by the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Section 21 enlarges his authority in an emergency and s. 13(e) gives him an indemnity for what he spent.

options.text: The firm is bound only if the other partners later ratify the hiring in writing
options.explanation: Ratification would bind the firm in any case; s. 21 makes it unnecessary in a genuine emergency.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 22 · Acts done in the firm name
questions.stem: A partner of a trading firm borrows ₹3,00,000 from a moneylender for the firm's use and signs the promissory note in his own personal name only. On the note:

readLink.label: Read: Extending and restricting authority, ss. 20 to 24 →

options.text: The firm is bound, because borrowing is within the implied authority of a partner in a trading firm
options.explanation: Borrowing is within implied authority, but s. 22 is a separate and additional requirement about how the act is done.

options.text: The firm is not bound, because to bind the firm an instrument must be executed in the firm name or in a manner expressing an intention to bind the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Section 22 fixes the manner of the act, and a note signed personally binds the partner alone.

options.text: The firm is bound, because the money was in fact used for the firm's business
options.explanation: Use of the money may found a claim in restitution against the firm, but it does not make the firm a party to the note.

options.text: Both the firm and the partner are bound jointly and severally under section 25
options.explanation: Section 25 attaches to acts of the firm; a note signed in a personal name is not an act of the firm.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 25 · Nature of a partner's liability
questions.stem: The liability of a partner for the acts of the firm done while he is a partner is:

readLink.label: Read: Liability of the firm and its partners, ss. 25 to 27 →

options.text: Joint only, so that all the partners must be sued together
options.explanation: Section 25 adds 'and also severally', which permits a suit against a single partner for the whole debt.

options.text: Several only, each partner being liable for his profit-sharing proportion of the debt
options.explanation: Profit-sharing governs contribution between the partners; it does not limit what a creditor may recover from any one of them.

options.text: Limited to the capital each partner has agreed to contribute
options.explanation: That is the position of a shareholder in a limited company, not of a partner in a firm.

options.text: Joint with the other partners and also several, and unlimited
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25 uses both words, so a creditor may sue all the partners or any one of them for the whole amount.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 27 · Misapplication by a partner
questions.stem: A client hands ₹4,00,000 to one partner of a firm of consultants, for investment through the firm, and that partner pockets it without the money ever reaching the firm's books. The firm is:

readLink.label: Read: Liability of the firm and its partners, ss. 25 to 27 →

options.text: Not liable, because the money never entered the custody of the firm
options.explanation: Custody of the firm is the requirement of s. 27(b); clause (a) covers exactly the case where the money never reaches the firm.

options.text: Not liable, because a dishonest misappropriation cannot be an act done in the business of the firm
options.explanation: Sections 26 and 27 exist for wrongful acts; the test is apparent authority or the ordinary course of business, not honesty.

options.text: Liable to make good the loss, because a partner acting within his apparent authority received the money and misapplied it
options.explanation: Correct. This is s. 27(a): the money came in on the strength of his apparent authority, so the firm bears the loss and may recover from him.

options.text: Liable only to the extent of the defaulting partner's share in the firm's property
options.explanation: The firm is liable to make good the whole loss; adjustment against the wrongdoer's share is an internal matter.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 33 · Expulsion of a partner
questions.stem: An expulsion of a partner by a majority is valid only if:

readLink.label: Read: Changes in the constitution, ss. 31 to 38 →

options.text: A majority of the partners resolve to expel him, whether or not the deed confers such a power
options.explanation: Section 33(1) begins by saying a partner may NOT be expelled by any majority save in exercise of a power conferred by contract.

options.text: The expelled partner is given a share of the firm's goodwill as compensation
options.explanation: No such payment is required by s. 33; what matters is the source of the power and the good faith of its exercise.

options.text: The expulsion is registered with the Registrar of Firms before it takes effect
options.explanation: Notifying the Registrar keeps the register current under s. 63; it is not a condition of a valid expulsion.

options.text: The power to expel is conferred by contract between the partners, it is exercised by a majority, and it is exercised in good faith
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions in s. 33(1) must be satisfied; an expulsion failing any of them is void and the partner remains a partner.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 35 · Estate of a deceased partner
questions.stem: The deed provides that the firm shall not be dissolved by the death of a partner. A partner dies in March 2026 and the firm continues. For debts incurred by the firm in June 2026, his estate is:

readLink.label: Read: Changes in the constitution, ss. 31 to 38 →

options.text: Not liable, because the estate of a deceased partner is not liable for any act of the firm done after his death
options.explanation: Correct. Section 35 protects the estate for post-death acts, and no public notice of the death is required.

options.text: Liable, until public notice of the death is given under section 72
options.explanation: Public notice is not required on death; the estate's protection under s. 35 is automatic.

options.text: Liable, because the firm continued in the same name with the same business
options.explanation: Continuation of the firm does not extend the estate's exposure to acts done after the death.

options.text: Liable to the extent of the deceased partner's share, though not beyond it
options.explanation: The estate is free from post-death acts altogether; its share may still answer for debts incurred before the death.

questions.stem: Dinesh retired on 1 April 2026, his share in the property of the firm being ₹8,00,000. No final settlement was made and the firm continued to use his share. For the year to 31 March 2027 the profits attributable to the use of his share are ₹57,000. Under section 37, the maximum Dinesh can claim for that year is:

readLink.label: Read: The outgoing partner, ss. 36 and 37 →

options.explanation: This assumes he is confined to the 6% interest. Section 37 gives him an option, and the profit figure is higher here.
Correct. He may take either the profits attributable to the use of his share (₹57,000) or 6% p.a. interest (₹8,00,000 × 6% = ₹48,000); the higher of the two is ₹57,000.
This adds the profits and the interest together. The section gives an option between them, not both.
This treats him as entitled only to the excess of the profits over the interest, which is not what s. 37 provides.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the particulars required to be stated in the statement filed with the Registrar under section 58?

readLink.label: Read: Registration of firms, ss. 58 and 59 →

options.text: The date on which each partner joined the firm
options.explanation: This particular is expressly required by s. 58(1), and it is the one students most often forget.

options.text: The names in full and permanent addresses of the partners
options.explanation: Section 58(1) requires precisely this particular.

options.text: The amount of capital contributed by each partner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 58 requires the firm name, the principal and other places of business, the date each partner joined, the partners' names and permanent addresses, and the duration — capital is not among them.

options.text: The duration of the firm
options.explanation: Section 58(1) requires the duration of the firm to be stated.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 69(2) · Suit by an unregistered firm
questions.stem: An unregistered firm wishes to sue a customer for ₹7,50,000 due under a supply contract. It:

readLink.label: Read: Effect of non-registration, s. 69 →

options.text: May institute the suit, since registration is optional under the Act
options.explanation: Registration is optional, but s. 69 is the sanction: the price of not registering is the loss of the right to sue on a contract.

options.text: May institute the suit and register the firm while it is pending, which cures the defect
options.explanation: The bar attaches to the institution of the suit, so registering midway does not save a suit already filed.

options.text: May institute the suit only if the amount claimed exceeds ₹1,00,000
options.explanation: The only monetary relief in s. 69 works the other way: small claims not exceeding ₹100 are outside the bar.

options.text: Cannot institute the suit; it must first register and have the suing partners shown in the Register of Firms
options.explanation: Correct. Section 69(2) bars a suit by or on behalf of an unregistered firm against a third party to enforce a contractual right.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 69(3) · Set-off and saved suits
questions.stem: An unregistered firm is sued by its landlord for ₹2,20,000 of rent. The firm wishes to set off ₹90,000 that the landlord owes it under a separate contract, and one partner separately wishes to sue for dissolution of the firm. Which is correct?

readLink.label: Read: What non-registration does not stop, s. 69 →

options.text: Both the set-off and the suit for dissolution are barred
options.explanation: This misses the saving in s. 69(3)(a) for dissolution, accounts of a dissolved firm, and realisation of its property.

options.text: The set-off is barred but the suit for dissolution may be filed
options.explanation: Correct. Section 69(3) extends the bar to a claim of set-off, while s. 69(3)(a) expressly saves a suit for dissolution.

options.text: Both the set-off and the suit for dissolution may proceed
options.explanation: Section 69(3) applies the bar to a claim of set-off in as many words, so the set-off cannot proceed.

options.text: The set-off may proceed but the dissolution suit is barred
options.explanation: This reverses both rules: it is the set-off that is barred and the dissolution suit that is saved.

questions.stem: A supplier who has not been paid by an unregistered firm wants to sue the firm and its partners. He:

readLink.label: Read: What non-registration does not stop, s. 69 →

options.text: May sue, because section 69 does not affect the right of a third party to sue the firm or its partners
options.explanation: Correct. The bar in s. 69 runs one way only: it disables the firm and its partners as plaintiffs, not its creditors.

options.text: May not sue until the firm registers itself under section 59
options.explanation: The supplier has no power to make the firm register, and the Act does not put his remedy at the firm's mercy.

options.text: May sue the firm but not the individual partners
options.explanation: Section 25 makes every partner jointly and severally liable, and s. 69 does not touch that.

options.text: May sue only for an amount not exceeding ₹100
options.explanation: The ₹100 limit is an exception to the bar on suits BY a firm; it has nothing to do with a third party's claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following brings about a COMPULSORY dissolution of a firm, which the partners cannot avoid by agreement?

readLink.label: Read: Modes of dissolution, ss. 40 to 43 →

options.text: The death of a partner
options.explanation: Death is a contingency under s. 42(c) and the section is expressly subject to contract, so a deed may keep the firm alive.

options.text: The happening of an event which makes it unlawful for the business of the firm to be carried on
options.explanation: Correct. Section 41(b) operates regardless of the deed, subject only to the proviso for a firm with several separate lawful adventures.

options.text: The expiry of the fixed term for which the firm was constituted
options.explanation: Expiry of the term is a s. 42(a) contingency, again subject to contract, and the partners may simply carry on at will.

options.text: The retirement of a partner with the consent of all the others
options.explanation: Retirement changes the constitution of the firm under s. 32; it does not dissolve the firm at all.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 44 · Grounds for dissolution by the court
questions.stem: A partner petitions the court to dissolve the firm, relying on his own repeated breaches of the partnership agreement, which have made working together impossible. The petition on that ground will:

readLink.label: Read: Dissolution by the court, s. 44 →

options.text: Succeed, because persistent breach of the agreement is a ground expressly listed in section 44
options.explanation: The ground is listed, but its wording confines it to breaches by a partner other than the one bringing the suit.

options.text: Succeed, because the court may dissolve a firm on any ground which makes it just and equitable to do so
options.explanation: The just and equitable ground exists in s. 44(g), but it cannot be used to reward a petitioner relying on his own wrongdoing.

options.text: Fail, because the ground of persistent breach is available only against a partner other than the partner suing
options.explanation: Correct. Grounds (b) to (e) of s. 44 all carry the words 'other than the partner suing'; a partner cannot rely on his own default.

options.text: Fail, because the court has no power to dissolve a firm before the expiry of its fixed term
options.explanation: The court's power under s. 44 is not limited by the term of the firm; the objection here is the identity of the defaulting partner.

questions.stem: A firm is dissolved but no public notice is given. A former partner then takes goods on credit in the firm's name from an old supplier. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Liability after dissolution, s. 45 →

options.text: The partners remain liable to the supplier, because liability for acts that would have been acts of the firm continues until public notice of the dissolution is given
options.explanation: Correct. Section 45(1) keeps the partners liable to outsiders until public notice, and any partner may give that notice.

options.text: No partner is liable, because the authority of every partner ends automatically on dissolution
options.explanation: Authority ends for new business as between the partners, but s. 45 protects an outsider who had no notice of the dissolution.

options.text: Only the partner who took the goods is liable, because the firm no longer exists
options.explanation: The absence of public notice is exactly what makes the others liable as well.

options.text: The partners are liable only if the firm was registered and the dissolution was not notified to the Registrar
options.explanation: The requirement of public notice under s. 45 applies to registered and unregistered firms alike.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 48(b) · Order of application of assets
questions.stem: In settling accounts after dissolution, the assets of the firm are applied in which order?

readLink.label: Read: Settlement of accounts, s. 48 →

options.text: Partners' capital, then partners' advances, then debts of the firm to third parties, then the residue equally
options.explanation: This reverses the whole order and would pay the partners before the firm's creditors.

options.text: Debts of the firm to third parties, then partners' capital, then partners' advances, then the residue in the profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: Advances rank ahead of capital, not behind it; a loan by a partner is a debt of the firm to him.

options.text: Partners' advances, then debts of the firm to third parties, then capital, then the residue equally
options.explanation: Outside creditors come first, and the residue is divided in the profit-sharing ratio, not equally.

options.text: Debts of the firm to third parties, then partners' advances, then partners' capital, then the residue in the profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: Correct. That is the order laid down in s. 48(b), and a partner's loan ranks above capital but below outside creditors.

questions.stem: On dissolution a firm's assets realise ₹47,00,000. Outside creditors are owed ₹18,00,000. Deepa had advanced ₹5,00,000 to the firm over and above her capital. Capitals are Deepa ₹9,00,000, Elango ₹6,00,000 and Farhan ₹3,00,000, and profits are shared 3 : 2 : 1. The total Deepa receives is:

readLink.label: Read: Settlement of accounts, s. 48 →

options.explanation: This pays her capital and her residue share but forgets that her ₹5,00,000 advance is repaid before any capital under s. 48(b)(ii).
This repays the advance and the capital but omits her 3/6 share of the ₹6,00,000 residue.
This divides the residue equally rather than in the 3 : 2 : 1 profit-sharing ratio required by s. 48(b)(iv).

Correct. Assets 47,00,000 less creditors 18,00,000 = 29,00,000; less her advance 5,00,000 = 24,00,000; less capitals 18,00,000 = residue 6,00,000, of which her 3/6 share is 3,00,000. Total 5,00,000 + 9,00,000 + 3,00,000.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 48(b) · Assets insufficient for capital
questions.stem: On dissolution a firm's assets realise ₹27,00,000. Outside creditors are owed ₹15,00,000 and partner P had advanced ₹3,00,000 beyond his capital. Capitals are P ₹8,00,000 and Q ₹4,00,000. On account of capital, Q receives:

readLink.label: Read: Settlement of accounts, s. 48 →

options.explanation: This repays Q's capital in full and leaves the whole shortfall on P; s. 48(b)(iii) requires capital to be repaid rateably.
This divides the ₹9,00,000 equally between the two partners instead of rateably in the ratio of their capitals.
Correct. After creditors and the advance, ₹9,00,000 is left against capitals of ₹12,00,000, so capital is repaid rateably: Q gets 4/12 × 9,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.
This applies the shortfall of ₹3,00,000 wholly to Q, which neither s. 48(b) nor the rateable rule supports.

questions.stem: The goodwill of a dissolved firm is sold to an outside buyer. In the absence of any agreement, a former partner may:

readLink.label: Read: Settlement of accounts, s. 48 →

options.text: Not carry on any competing business, since the goodwill has been sold
options.explanation: The sale of goodwill does not, without an express restraint, prevent competition; it prevents passing off and soliciting old customers.

options.text: Carry on a competing business and advertise it, but may not use the firm name, represent himself as carrying on the business of the firm, or solicit customers who dealt with the firm before its dissolution
options.explanation: Correct. Section 55(2) and (3) permit competition and advertising while forbidding those three things.

options.text: Carry on a competing business and solicit the firm's old customers, provided he does not use the firm name
options.explanation: Soliciting persons who were dealing with the firm before dissolution is expressly barred alongside the use of the firm name.

options.text: Carry on a competing business only if he first offers the buyer a right of first refusal
options.explanation: The Act imposes no such requirement; the only permissible fetter is a reasonable agreed restraint.

questions.stem: Which of the following is required for a valid 'public notice' by a registered firm on the retirement of a partner?

readLink.label: Read: Public notice, s. 72 →

options.text: Publication in the Official Gazette, publication in at least one vernacular newspaper circulating in the district of the firm's principal place of business, and notice to the Registrar of Firms
options.explanation: Correct. Section 72 requires all the applicable limbs; for a registered firm the notice to the Registrar under s. 63 is one of them.

options.text: Publication in the Official Gazette alone
options.explanation: A Gazette notice by itself is incomplete: the vernacular newspaper and, for a registered firm, the Registrar are also required.

options.text: Individual written notice to every person who has dealt with the firm in the last three years
options.explanation: The Act prescribes a form of public notice; it does not require individual notices to past customers.

options.text: A notice displayed at the firm's principal place of business for thirty days
options.explanation: Displaying a notice at the premises is not one of the modes prescribed by s. 72.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 4, 6, 28 · Case: who is a partner in the garment unit
questions.case: Nalini runs a garment unit at Tiruppur. Omkar lends her ₹15,00,000 for the business and, instead of fixed interest, is paid 20% of the annual profits until the loan is repaid; he takes no part in the business and no supplier has heard of him. Priya is the unit's manager, paid ₹55,000 a month plus 10% of the net profits, and works under Nalini's directions. Rakesh sold Nalini the goodwill of his own tailoring business, the price being payable as 12% of the profits for three years. Nalini's letterhead has for two years described Rakesh as 'Partner (Advisory)'; Rakesh has seen it on several occasions and has never objected. In January 2026 a fabric supplier, who had earlier refused the unit credit, supplies ₹11,00,000 of cloth on credit after being shown that letterhead and being told that Rakesh stands behind the business. The unit defaults.

readLink.label: Read: Deciding whether a partnership exists, s. 6 →

questions.stem: Omkar's position in relation to the unit is that he is:

options.text: A partner, because he shares the profits of a business carried on by Nalini
options.explanation: This treats profit-sharing as conclusive, which the Explanation to s. 6 forbids.

options.text: Not a partner, because the receipt of a share of profits by a lender does not of itself make him a partner
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 6 names the lender, and Omkar has no power to bind the business.

options.text: A partner in profits only, liable to third parties but not for losses
options.explanation: A partner in profits only is a member of the firm; Omkar's share is simply the return on his loan.

options.text: A sub-partner, because his return is measured by the profits of the business
options.explanation: A sub-partnership arises where a partner shares his own share with a stranger; Omkar deals with the proprietor, not with any partner's share.

questions.stem: Priya's position is that she is:

options.text: A partner, since a 10% share of net profits is a share in the business itself
options.explanation: The size or form of the share is not the test; the absence of mutual agency is decisive.

options.text: A nominal partner, because outsiders know she manages the unit
options.explanation: A nominal partner is one held out as a partner; managing a business is not holding out.

options.text: A servant of the business remunerated in part by a share of profits, and therefore not a partner
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 6 covers a servant or agent remunerated by a share of profits, and she works under direction.

options.text: A partner by holding out under section 28
options.explanation: Nothing represents Priya as a partner, and s. 28 requires a representation acted upon by the person giving credit.

questions.stem: As against the fabric supplier, Rakesh is:

options.text: Liable as a partner, because he knowingly permitted himself to be represented as a partner and the supplier gave credit on the faith of that representation
options.explanation: Correct. Two years of silence with knowledge is 'knowingly permitting', and the credit was given after the letterhead was shown.

options.text: Not liable, because a person who merely sold goodwill and takes a share of profits is not a partner under section 6
options.explanation: Section 6 answers whether he is a partner; s. 28 fixes him with liability to an outsider even though he is not one.

options.text: Liable only to the extent of the 12% profit share he has already received
options.explanation: Liability under s. 28 is liability as a partner for the debt, not a refund of what he received.

options.text: Not liable, because he never told the supplier anything himself
options.explanation: Section 28 covers a person who knowingly permits himself to be represented, and it does not matter that he did not know the representation had reached this supplier.

questions.stem: Having been held liable, Rakesh claims a share in the profits and the right to inspect the accounts. He is:
questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 28 · Rights of a holding-out partner

options.text: Entitled to both, because a person liable as a partner must be treated as a partner for all purposes
options.explanation: The section makes him liable 'as a partner' to the person who gave credit; it does not admit him to the firm.

options.text: Entitled to inspect the accounts but not to any share of profits
options.explanation: Even the narrower right of inspection belongs to partners under s. 12(d) and to a minor under s. 30(2), not to a holding-out partner.

options.text: Entitled to a share of profits from the date the supplier gave credit
options.explanation: No profit entitlement arises at any date; s. 28 creates no interest in the business.

options.text: Entitled to neither, because section 28 imposes liability by estoppel and confers no rights against the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Holding out is a one-way rule: liability to the outsider, no membership rights.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30 · Case: the minor's election timeline
questions.case: With the consent of all four partners of M/s Konark Traders, Vivek was admitted to the benefits of partnership on 5 September 2021, when he was 13, with a one-tenth share of the profits. Vivek attained majority on 18 November 2025. He was studying abroad and his guardian told him about the admission only on 3 February 2026, when the papers were handed over. Vivek has given no notice of any kind. On 12 May 2026 a bank sues all the partners personally on a term loan the firm took in December 2022 and has now defaulted on.

readLink.label: Read: The six-month election, s. 30(5) →

questions.stem: The last date on which Vivek may give public notice of his election is:

options.explanation: This runs the six months from the date of majority and ignores the later date of knowledge, which s. 30(5) requires to be taken.

options.text: 3 August 2026
options.explanation: Correct. The six months run from the later of majority (18 November 2025) and knowledge (3 February 2026), so they expire six months after 3 February 2026.

options.text: 5 March 2022
options.explanation: This runs the period from the date of admission to the benefits, which is not a trigger under s. 30(5).

options.text: 3 February 2027
options.explanation: This allows twelve months from the date of knowledge; the section gives six.

questions.stem: On 12 May 2026, when the bank sues, Vivek's exposure is:
questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30(3) · Position before the window closes

options.text: He is personally liable, because he has already attained majority
options.explanation: Attaining majority starts the election clock; it does not by itself convert him into a partner.

options.text: He has no liability at all, because the loan was taken while he was a minor
options.explanation: His share was liable for the acts of the firm from the date he was admitted to the benefits, including the 2022 loan.

options.text: His share in the property and profits of the firm is liable, but he is not personally liable
options.explanation: Correct. Until the six months expire he remains a person admitted to the benefits, and s. 30(3) protects him personally.

options.text: His guardian is personally liable, having consented to his admission
options.explanation: The guardian's consent does not make the guardian a partner or a surety.

questions.stem: If Vivek lets the six months pass without giving any notice, he becomes a partner and his personal liability to third parties runs from:
questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30(5) and 30(7) · Effect of silence

options.text: 18 November 2025, the date he attained majority
options.explanation: Majority governs the election window, not the reach of the liability, which the section takes back to the date of admission.

options.text: 3 February 2026, the date he learned of his admission
options.explanation: Knowledge fixes the start of the six months only; it has no bearing on the period of liability.

options.text: The date on which the six months expire, since he becomes a partner only then
options.explanation: He does become a partner then, but s. 30(7)(b) expressly backdates his liability.

options.text: 5 September 2021, the date he was admitted to the benefits of partnership
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(7)(b) makes him personally liable for all acts of the firm done since he was admitted to the benefits.

questions.stem: The bank disputes that Vivek learned of his admission only on 3 February 2026. Who must prove the date of knowledge?

options.text: Vivek, because the burden of proving that he had no knowledge until a particular date lies on the person asserting that fact
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(6) puts the burden on the person asserting the want of knowledge.

options.text: The bank, because it is the plaintiff and must prove its case
options.explanation: The general rule about plaintiffs is displaced by the specific rule in s. 30(6).

options.text: The other partners, who admitted him to the benefits
options.explanation: They are not the persons asserting want of knowledge, so the burden does not fall on them.

options.text: His guardian, who received the papers on his behalf
options.explanation: The section speaks of the person asserting the fact, and the assertion here is Vivek's.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 69 · Case: who may sue when the firm is unregistered
questions.case: M/s Deccan Agencies is a firm of three partners — Sanjay, Tara and Umesh — which has never been registered under Chapter VII of the Indian Partnership Act 1932. Four disputes arise in 2026. First, the firm wants to sue a customer for ₹9,80,000 due under a supply contract. Second, its landlord sues the firm for ₹3,40,000 of arrears of rent, and the firm wants to set off ₹1,15,000 which the landlord admittedly owes it under a separate printing contract. Third, Umesh wants to sue Sanjay and Tara for his share of the profits under the deed. Fourth, Umesh wants, in the alternative, to sue for dissolution of the firm and for accounts of the dissolved firm.

readLink.label: Read: Effect of non-registration, s. 69 →

questions.stem: The firm's suit against the customer for ₹9,80,000:
questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 69(2) · Firm suing a third party

options.text: May be instituted, because the customer's liability arises from a completed supply and not from the partnership
options.explanation: The bar looks at who is suing and on what; a contract claim by an unregistered firm is caught however clear the debt.

options.text: Cannot be instituted, because a suit by an unregistered firm against a third party to enforce a contractual right is barred
options.explanation: Correct. Section 69(2) requires the firm to be registered and the suing partners to be shown in the Register of Firms.

options.text: May be instituted by any one partner in his own name, since the bar applies only to suits in the firm name
options.explanation: Section 69(2) applies to a suit 'by or on behalf of' the firm, so suing in a partner's name does not escape it.

options.text: May be instituted if the firm registers itself before the first hearing
options.explanation: The bar attaches to the institution of the suit, so registration after filing does not cure it.

questions.stem: In the landlord's suit, the amount the firm must pay if the landlord proves his claim is:

options.text: ₹2,25,000, being the rent less the amount the landlord owes the firm
options.explanation: This allows the set-off of ₹1,15,000, which s. 69(3) expressly bars for an unregistered firm.

options.text: Nil, because an unregistered firm cannot be sued at all
options.explanation: Section 69 does not affect a third party's right to sue the firm; the landlord's claim proceeds normally.

options.text: ₹3,40,000, because the bar in section 69 extends to a claim of set-off
options.explanation: Correct. The landlord's suit is unaffected by s. 69, but the firm cannot set off its ₹1,15,000 claim, so the full ₹3,40,000 is payable.

options.text: ₹1,15,000, because only the disputed portion of the claim survives the bar
options.explanation: The bar removes the firm's counter-claim entirely; it does not reduce the landlord's claim to the disputed amount.

questions.stem: Umesh's suit against Sanjay and Tara for his share of the profits:
questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 69(1) · Partner suing a co-partner

options.text: Is barred, because a person suing as a partner cannot sue the firm or a co-partner to enforce a right arising from contract unless the firm is registered and he is shown in the Register of Firms
options.explanation: Correct. Section 69(1) sets both conditions, and neither is satisfied here.

options.text: Is maintainable, because section 69 protects only third parties dealing with the firm
options.explanation: Section 69(1) is aimed precisely at a partner suing the firm or a co-partner.

options.text: Is maintainable, because a claim for a share of profits arises under the Act and not under a contract
options.explanation: Section 69(1) covers rights arising from a contract AND rights conferred by the Act, so both routes are closed.

options.text: Is barred only if Sanjay and Tara raise the objection in their written statement
options.explanation: The bar goes to the institution of the suit and is not a matter of pleading it as a defence.

questions.stem: Umesh's alternative suit for dissolution of the firm and for accounts of the dissolved firm:

options.text: Is barred, because the firm is unregistered and Umesh is suing as a partner
options.explanation: That is the general rule in s. 69(1), but s. 69(3)(a) carves out dissolution and accounts of a dissolved firm.

options.text: May be instituted only after the firm has been registered under section 59
options.explanation: Registration is unnecessary for a saved suit; that is what the exception is for.

options.text: May be instituted for dissolution but not for accounts of the dissolved firm
options.explanation: Both are named in the exception, together with realisation of the property of the dissolved firm.

options.text: May be instituted, because section 69(3)(a) saves suits for dissolution, for accounts of a dissolved firm and for realisation of the property of a dissolved firm
options.explanation: Correct. This is the standard route out for a partner of an unregistered firm.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 4, 6 · Essentials and the true test
questions.stem: State the essential elements of a partnership under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 and explain how the existence of a partnership is determined where the parties dispute it. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The five essentials and mutual agency, s. 4 →

skeleton.point: Definition: partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all; partners individually, firm collectively, firm name is the trading style

Essential 1 and 2 — an association of two or more persons competent to contract (maximum 50 under s. 464 of the Companies Act 2013), and an agreement, since partnership arises from contract and not from status
Essential 3 and 4 — a business (which includes every trade, occupation and profession, and may be a single adventure) and an agreement to share its profits; loss-sharing is not essential
Essential 5 — mutual agency: the business must be carried on by all or any of them acting for all, each partner being both principal and agent; this is the true test
Determination of existence — regard shall be had to the real relation between the parties as shown by all relevant facts taken together; the label the parties use is not decisive

Profit-sharing is not conclusive — the Explanation excludes a lender, a servant or agent remunerated by a share of profits, a widow or child of a deceased partner taking an annuity, and a seller of goodwill taking a share of profits as the price

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 30 · Position of a minor
questions.stem: Explain the position of a minor admitted to the benefits of partnership, both during his minority and on his attaining majority. (8 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Minor admitted to the benefits, s. 30 →

skeleton.point: A minor cannot be a partner because his agreement is void, but with the consent of all the partners for the time being he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership in an existing firm

Rights during minority — a share in the property and profits of the firm as agreed, and access to, inspection and copies of any of the ACCOUNTS of the firm (contrast a partner's right to any of the books)
Liability during minority — his share is liable for the acts of the firm, but he is not personally liable

Disabilities — he cannot take part in management, cannot bind the firm, and may sue for his share of the property or profits only when severing his connection with the firm, the value being determined as on the date of severance

Election on majority — within six months of attaining majority, or of obtaining knowledge that he had been admitted to the benefits, whichever date is later, he may give PUBLIC NOTICE electing to become or not to become a partner
Failure to give notice — he becomes a partner in the firm on the expiry of the six months; the burden of proving want of knowledge until a particular date lies on the person asserting it

If he becomes a partner — his share remains as before and he becomes personally liable to third parties for all acts of the firm done since he was admitted to the benefits; if he elects not to become a partner, his rights and liabilities continue only up to the date of the public notice and he may sue for his share

questions.stem: What is the implied authority of a partner? State the acts which, in the absence of any usage or custom of trade to the contrary, fall outside it. (7 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Implied authority, s. 19 →

skeleton.point: A partner is the agent of the firm for the purposes of its business; the act of a partner done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm binds the firm, and this authority is called his implied authority

Conditions — the act must relate to the normal business of the firm, must be done in the usual way, and must be done in the firm name or in a manner expressing or implying an intention to bind the firm

Acts outside implied authority: submit a dispute relating to the business to arbitration; open a banking account on behalf of the firm in his own name; compromise or relinquish any claim or part of a claim by the firm; withdraw a suit or proceeding filed on behalf of the firm

Acts outside implied authority (continued): admit any liability in a suit or proceeding against the firm; acquire immovable property on behalf of the firm; transfer immovable property belonging to the firm; enter into partnership on behalf of the firm

The list applies only in the absence of a usage or custom of trade to the contrary; the partners may extend or restrict implied authority by contract, but a restriction does not bind a third party who does not know of it, and in an emergency a partner may do what a person of ordinary prudence would do to protect the firm from loss

questions.stem: Registration of a firm under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 is optional. Discuss the consequences of non-registration and the cases in which those consequences do not apply. (8 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Effect of non-registration, s. 69 →

skeleton.point: Registration is optional and carries no penalty; it is effected by filing a statement in the prescribed form with the Registrar and is complete when the Registrar records an entry of the statement in the Register of Firms

A partner cannot sue the firm or any person alleged to be or to have been a partner to enforce a right arising from a contract or conferred by the Act, unless the firm is registered AND the person suing is or has been shown in the Register of Firms as a partner
The firm cannot sue a third party to enforce a right arising from a contract unless the same two conditions are satisfied
The same bar applies to a claim of set-off and to any other proceeding to enforce a right arising from a contract; registration after the suit has been instituted does not cure the defect
Exception — the right of a third party to sue the firm or its partners is not affected; the bar operates one way only

Exceptions — suits for the dissolution of the firm, for accounts of a dissolved firm, and for the realisation of the property of a dissolved firm; and the powers of an Official Assignee, Receiver or Court under the insolvency law to realise the property of an insolvent partner

Exceptions — suits and claims of value not exceeding one hundred rupees and proceedings incidental to them; firms and partners in areas notified under s. 56; and claims arising otherwise than out of a contract, such as an action in tort or for infringement of the firm's trade mark

questions.stem: Distinguish between dissolution of partnership and dissolution of a firm, and state the modes in which a firm may be dissolved. (7 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Modes of dissolution, ss. 40 to 43 →

skeleton.point: The dissolution of partnership between ALL the partners of a firm is called the dissolution of the firm; where only some partners cease to be partners and the business continues, the partnership is dissolved but the firm is not

Consequences of the distinction — on dissolution of the firm the business is wound up, the assets are realised and the accounts finally settled, whereas on a mere change in the constitution the firm continues; every dissolution of a firm involves dissolution of partnership, but not the converse
Dissolution by agreement — with the consent of all the partners or in accordance with a contract between them

Compulsory dissolution — by the adjudication of all the partners, or of all the partners but one, as insolvent, or by the happening of an event making it unlawful for the business to be carried on, subject to the proviso for separate lawful adventures
Dissolution on the happening of contingencies, subject to contract — expiry of a fixed term, completion of the adventure, death of a partner, or adjudication of a partner as insolvent

Dissolution by notice in a partnership at will — any partner may give notice in writing to all the others, the firm being dissolved from the date named in the notice or, if none is named, from the date of communication

Dissolution by the court at the suit of a partner — insanity, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of the whole interest, business only at a loss, or any other just and equitable ground; grounds (b) to (e) relate to a partner other than the partner suing

questions.stem: State the rules for the settlement of accounts between partners after the dissolution of a firm, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Settlement of accounts, s. 48 →

skeleton.point: Every partner is entitled to have the property of the firm applied in payment of the debts and liabilities of the firm and to have the surplus distributed among the partners according to their rights

Losses, including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in the proportions in which they were entitled to share profits
The assets of the firm, including any sums contributed by partners to make up deficiencies of capital, are applied first in paying the debts of the firm to third parties

Next in paying to each partner rateably what is due to him from the firm for advances as distinguished from capital, and then in paying to each partner rateably what is due to him on account of capital
The residue, if any, is divided among the partners in the proportions in which they were entitled to share profits

Firm property is applied first in payment of the debts of the firm and any surplus in payment of the partners' separate debts; a partner's separate property is applied first in payment of his separate debts and the surplus towards the firm's debts

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 32 to 37 · The outgoing partner
questions.stem: Explain the rights and liabilities of an outgoing partner, including his position where the firm continues to use his share without a final settlement of accounts. (7 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The outgoing partner, ss. 36 and 37 →

skeleton.point: A partner may retire with the consent of all the other partners, in accordance with an express agreement, or, where the partnership is at will, by notice in writing to all the other partners

He remains liable to third parties for acts of the firm done before his retirement unless discharged by an agreement with the third party and the partners of the reconstituted firm, which may be implied by a course of dealing after the third party knew of the retirement

He and the other partners continue to be liable to third parties for acts done after retirement until PUBLIC NOTICE is given, which may be given by him or by any partner; a partner not known to the person dealing with the firm to be a partner is not so liable

Right to compete — he may carry on a business competing with that of the firm and advertise it, but may not use the firm name, represent himself as carrying on the business of the firm, or solicit the custom of persons who were dealing with the firm before he ceased to be a partner

An agreement restraining him from carrying on a similar business within a specified period or specified local limits is valid if the restrictions are reasonable, notwithstanding s. 27 of the Contract Act

Where the continuing partners carry on the business with the firm's property without a final settlement of accounts, he or his estate is entitled AT HIS OPTION to the share of profits since he ceased to be a partner attributable to the use of his share of the property, or to interest at six per cent per annum on the amount of his share in the property
Where the continuing partners had a contractual option to purchase his interest and it has been duly exercised in all material respects, he is not entitled to any further share of profits
